title: The History of Mortal Kombat | From the 1992 Arcade to Mortal Kombat 1 | Gaming History
description: The full history of Mortal Kombat: Ed Boon and John Tobias, the 1992 arcade original, Mortal Monday, the ESRB, the 3D era, NetherRealm, Mortal Kombat 11, Mortal Kombat 1 and the Legacy Kollection.

sections.heading: Finish him
sections.script: Two fighters, a lot of blood and a voice that shouts finish him. Mortal Kombat is one of the most famous fighting game series ever made, and it is the best selling fighting game franchise in the world, with more than eighty million copies sold according to NetherRealm in twenty twenty three. It began as a small arcade game with digitized actors, it sparked a national debate in the United States, and it helped lead to the video game rating system we know today. In this video we walk through the complete history of Mortal Kombat: the arcade original in nineteen ninety two, the sequels that made it a hit, the move to three dimensions, the reboot of twenty eleven, and the latest games, including Mortal Kombat One. Get over here, and let's start.

sections.heading: Two creators and a deadline
sections.script: The story begins in nineteen ninety one at Midway Games. The company wanted a fighting game that could compete with the huge success of Street Fighter Two, and it gave the job to two developers, Ed Boon and John Tobias. They had about ten months, a small team and a budget of around one million dollars. John Tobias suggested using digitized footage of real actors instead of hand drawn sprites, which gave the characters a realistic look that was unusual at the time. An early idea based on Jean-Claude Van Damme fell through, but it lived on as a joke in the character Johnny Cage. Ho-Sung Pak played Liu Kang, and Daniel Pesina played Johnny Cage and Scorpion. The arcade game launched in August of nineteen ninety two.

sections.heading: Mortal Monday and the controversy
sections.script: The arcade game was a success, but the real explosion came on September thirteenth, nineteen ninety three. Acclaim released home versions for the Super Nintendo, the Sega Genesis, the Game Boy and the Game Gear, and the day was marketed as Mortal Monday. The game reportedly sold three million copies in its first three weeks. Its realistic looking violence and the fatality finishing moves also alarmed parents and politicians. Senators including Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl pushed the industry to act, and the controversy helped lead to the creation of the Entertainment Software Rating Board, better known as the ESRB. Today almost every game box in North America carries an ESRB rating, and Mortal Kombat played a major part in that story.

sections.heading: The arcade sequels
sections.script: Midway moved fast. Mortal Kombat Two arrived in the arcades in nineteen ninety three, followed by Mortal Kombat Three and Ultimate Mortal Kombat Three in nineteen ninety five. In nineteen ninety six came Mortal Kombat Trilogy, a big collection that packed more than thirty fighters into a single game and added a new finishing move called the Brutality. These were still two dimensional fighters built around digitized characters, and many fans remember them as the golden age of the series. Characters such as Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden, Kitana and Johnny Cage became icons. It was also a time when you could find a Mortal Kombat cabinet in almost every arcade, with crowds waiting for their turn to play.

sections.heading: A new dimension
sections.script: As the nineties ended, fighting games were moving into three dimensions, and Mortal Kombat followed. Mortal Kombat Four, released in nineteen ninety seven, brought the series into 3D, although critics felt it lagged behind Tekken Three, which launched the same year. After that the series moved from the arcade to home consoles. Mortal Kombat Deadly Alliance in two thousand two was the first all new Mortal Kombat produced exclusively for home consoles, and it was followed by Deception in two thousand four, which is remembered for bringing online play to the series. Behind the scenes, Midway Games filed for bankruptcy in February of two thousand nine. Warner Bros. bought most of its assets that same year, including the Mortal Kombat franchise, and the Chicago team became NetherRealm Studios in twenty ten.

sections.heading: The twenty eleven reboot
sections.script: Under Warner Bros., Ed Boon and his team made a fresh start. Mortal Kombat, released on April nineteenth, twenty eleven, is a soft reboot of the series. It returned to a two dimensional fighting style with modern three dimensional graphics. Players loved it, and it sold one million copies in its first month alone. It was the ninth main game in the series and proved that Mortal Kombat still had a huge audience more than a decade after its arcade peak. The series was back, and it was louder than ever. The new team at NetherRealm showed that the old arcade brand still had plenty of life, and fans on consoles and PC were ready to welcome it.

sections.heading: Mortal Kombat X and Mortal Kombat Eleven
sections.script: Next came Mortal Kombat X on April fourteenth, twenty fifteen. It sold more than ten million copies, with some reports citing eleven million, making it the fastest selling game in the franchise at the time. Then, on April twenty third, twenty nineteen, Mortal Kombat Eleven arrived on Switch, PlayStation 4, Windows and Xbox One. It was the best selling game in North America in April of that year and went on to sell more than fifteen million copies by twenty twenty two, which makes it the best selling title in the series. The Aftermath expansion followed on May twenty sixth, twenty twenty, adding story content, new characters and guests like RoboCop. Eleven also brought in famous guests such as the Joker, Spawn and the Terminator.

sections.heading: A new timeline with Mortal Kombat One
sections.script: In two thousand twenty three, NetherRealm rebooted the story again with Mortal Kombat One, in which Liu Kang creates a new timeline. The game added Kameo fighters, who are partner characters that jump in to help. It sold more than three million copies by January of twenty twenty four, four million by August of twenty twenty four, and Ed Boon announced five million in January of twenty twenty five. The Khaos Reigns expansion followed on September twenty fourth, twenty twenty four, with a new story involving the villain Titan Havik, free Animalities for all players and extra fighters such as Cyrax, Sektor, Noob Saibot, Ghostface, T-1000 and Conan the Barbarian. Mortal Kombat One sold more slowly than Eleven, but it remains the series' flagship.

sections.heading: Looking back with the Legacy Kollection
sections.script: The history of Mortal Kombat is now easy to play again. On October thirtieth, twenty twenty five, Atari and Digital Eclipse released Mortal Kombat Legacy Kollection on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, Switch Two, PC and other platforms. It collects eleven early titles, including the original Mortal Kombat, Mortal Kombat Two, Mortal Kombat Three, Ultimate Mortal Kombat Three with a rare WaveNet version, Mortal Kombat Four, Trilogy and Deadly Alliance. For longtime fans it is a trip down memory lane, and for new players it is a chance to see where it all began. After more than thirty years, Mortal Kombat is still one of the biggest names in fighting games, and its story is far from over.

sections.heading: Who is your favorite fighter
sections.script: From a ten month arcade project in nineteen ninety two to a franchise that has sold more than eighty million copies, Mortal Kombat has survived controversy, new technology and several reboots. It changed how games are rated, made the word fatality famous, and inspired a generation of fighting game players. So now we want to know. Which Mortal Kombat game is your favorite, the classic arcade era, the reboot, Eleven or Mortal Kombat One? And who is your all time favorite fighter, Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden or someone else? Tell us in the comments. If you enjoyed this history, like the video and subscribe for more gaming history, because there is a lot more to cover.
